synthesis.headline: Coverage is genuinely strong: of 189 merged cheatsheet items (~178 distinct after cross-agent dedupe), 128 are COVERED, 26 PARTIAL, 32 MISSING_OUT_OF_SYLLABUS (Stat 110-only machinery, chiefly MGFs, order statistics, and Stat 110's named-distribution zoo), and only 3 are MISSING_IN_SYLLABUS — i.e. in B&T/6.041 scope and genuinely absent. All three are small, one-paragraph repairs. In several places the notes are substantially deeper than the cheatsheet (Stirling derived rather than quoted, coupon collector with Euler asymptotics and Monte-Carlo, de Moivre-Laplace continuity correction, competing exponentials with the winner's identity, splitting/merging with the independence clause, mean recurrence times by first-step analysis). The real weakness is not content but retrieval surface: the distribution facts exist but are scattered across four tables in four different notes.

real_gaps.topic: Closure of the binomial under addition: X~Bin(n1,p), Y~Bin(n2,p) independent => X+Y ~ Bin(n1+n2,p)
real_gaps.why_it_matters: Two agents disagreed (one PARTIAL, one MISSING_IN_SYLLABUS); I re-ran the greps and took the MISSING verdict — no fragment states the additivity identity, only the Bernoulli-sum decomposition (g2_s5.html:153-154) from which a reader must re-derive it. It matters because the notes DO state every sibling closure by name — normal+normal (g3_s4.html:828 has its own subsection), Erlang+Exp (g5_s5.html:843), Poisson+Poisson via merging (G4 §4) — so a learner scanning for 'which families are closed under sums' finds a conspicuous hole exactly where the most-used discrete family should be. It is also the cheapest possible worked example of discrete convolution.
real_gaps.where_it_belongs: G3 §4 (g3_s4.html), the convolution subsections — as a short worked discrete convolution immediately before/after the Erlang and normal cases; cross-link from the binomial definition in G2 §1 (g2_s1.html) and from the sums-closure list at g3_s4.html:1150.

real_gaps.topic: Joint CDF F_{X,Y}(x,y)=P(X<=x, Y<=y), the 2-D CDF<->PDF link f=∂²F/∂x∂y, and the CDF-factorization criterion for independence
real_gaps.why_it_matters: B&T §3.4 states the joint CDF, so this is in scope, and one repair closes three separate audit items at once: the MISSING joint CDF, the PARTIAL 'mixed partial' (the identity appears exactly once, unflagged, mid-derivation at g4_s1.html:518 for f_{R,Θ} in a polar example), and the PARTIAL 'three equivalent independence conditions' (the CDF-factorization form is absent precisely because the object is never defined). I confirmed by grep: no fragment in notes/src/fragments contains 'joint CDF' or the P(X<=x,Y<=y) form. A learner who has internalized f=F' in one dimension (g3_s1.html:787) has no stated 2-D analogue, which bites on any max/min-of-two-variables problem attacked by the CDF method.
real_gaps.where_it_belongs: G3 §2 (g3_s2.html), §2.1 'The joint PDF, and probability as volume' — one short definition box plus the mixed-partial line, with a back-reference to G3 §1.4 (g3_s1.html:202) where the one-dimensional CDF is defined, and a third bullet added to the independence criteria in §2.4.

real_gaps.topic: Doubly stochastic chains: if every column of the transition matrix sums to 1, the uniform distribution is stationary
real_gaps.why_it_matters: Confirmed absent by grep ('doubly stochastic' -> zero hits across all 42 fragments). It is a one-line shortcut that lives entirely inside machinery G5 §3 already builds (balance equations plus normalization), and it saves solving the linear system outright on symmetric chains — a common exam time-saver. Genuinely in scope but low cost to omit; include it only as a remark, not a subsection.
real_gaps.where_it_belongs: G5 §3 (g5_s3.html), the balance-equations / steady-state section, as a one-sentence remark right after the balance equations plus normalization are set up.

One defn/thm box would close a dangling forward-reference.

The two-set version is fully proved and reused across six notes (g1_s1.html:100, :117-119). The three-set formula is absent; the only 'A ∪ B ∪ C' hit (g1_s1.html:119) is finite additivity for three DISJOINT pieces, which is a different statement and could mislead.

partials.topic: Reversibility / detailed balance as a general criterion
partials.what_is_thin: Both agents who touched this said PARTIAL, consistently. The cut/detailed-balance technique is well covered for birth-death and queueing chains (g5_s5.html:230), but 'reversible' is never defined — it appears once in scare quotes (g5_s3.html:586) inside a Gotcha warning that local balance is NOT general — and the theorem 'detailed balance => stationary' is never stated. B&T does not develop reversibility, so this is a soft gap, but the current treatment leaves the reader thinking local balance is a hack rather than a checkable sufficient condition.

partials.topic: Multinomial: lumping, conditional Multinomial, and the exact covariance
partials.what_is_thin: The multinomial coefficient and joint PMF are derived (g1_s4 §4.6, g7_s4), and the marginal fact N_k ~ Bin(n, θ_k) is stated in g7_s4. Missing: the lumping-closure property (merging categories keeps it multinomial), the conditional-Multinomial property, and the plain exact identity Cov(X_i,X_j) = -n p_i p_j. The negative covariance appears only in asymptotic normalized form inside the chi-square derivation (Σ = I - √θ√θᵀ). The exact identity is squarely in scope — G3 §4 covers covariance and G2 §5 covers indicator decompositions, which is exactly how you prove it.

The notes warn emphatically in the other direction — g3_s4 Gotcha: 'neither means independent', with Example 4.9 (Y=X²) — but never name the normal exception. The closest is g6_s4's jointly-normal LLMS theorem, which implies the ρ=0 case without saying it. Given how hard the notes hammer 'uncorrelated ≠ independent', one sentence naming the exception prevents an over-corrected misconception.
partials.where: G3 §4 (g3_s4.html, the covariance Gotcha) with a pointer to G6 §4

partials.topic: Hypergeometric variance and the finite-population correction

Since the notes use the hypergeometric as 'the standing counterexample when §1.4 tempts you to call every count binomial' (g2_s1.html:178), the variance is exactly where that contrast is sharpest — the correction factor IS the without-replacement penalty.

enrichment.topic: Universality of the Uniform (inverse-CDF transform): F(X)~Unif(0,1) and F^{-1}(U) has CDF F
enrichment.note: Best single enrichment candidate. Both agents who flagged it agreed it is out of B&T scope, but also agreed G3 §4 (g3_s4.html:27, the CDF method) already has every piece of machinery needed — it is a two-paragraph addition that pays off immediately as the basis of simulation, and it retroactively explains why the CDF method works at all. Worked with F(x)=1-e^{-x} it is also a clean self-check on the exponential material the notes already own.

Zero hits anywhere in the corpus. It is the single best cautionary tale about conditioning and would sit naturally at the end of G1 §2-§3, where conditional independence counterexamples in both directions are already worked (g1_s3.html:292-295, :537-559). Pure enrichment, high pedagogical return, no syllabus cost.

enrichment.topic: Moment generating functions — a short 'beyond the syllabus' appendix
enrichment.note: The largest structural difference between the two documents: the cheatsheet routes every sum-of-independents result through MGF multiplication; our notes route the same results through convolution (g3_s4) and process algebra (g4_s2, g4_s4). The notes already document the boundary deliberately (g4_s2.html:239-240 cites B&T's transform and says transforms are outside L12's scope). A two-page appendix showing M_{X+Y}=M_X·M_Y reproducing the Erlang and normal-sum results the reader already derived by convolution would make the exclusion legible rather than mysterious — and is the right home for the cheatsheet's MGF column.

enrichment.note: Zero hits for 'order statistic'. The notes already derive min and max by the CDF method (g3_s1.html:554, g7_s2.html:574-576) and already define the Beta family with mean/mode/variance (g3_s3, g3_s5:150-155), so the general ith-order-statistic density is a short step from material in hand and ties two existing threads together.

enrichment.topic: Two-dimensional change of variables via the Jacobian determinant
enrichment.note: The notes use the polar Jacobian ad hoc twice (g3_s1.html:583, g4_s1.html:500, 'the extra factor r is the Jacobian') without ever stating the general theorem, and they DO state the 1-D version (g3_s4.html:197). enrichment.topic: Random walk on an undirected graph: stationary distribution proportional to degree
enrichment.note: Out of B&T Chapter 7, but the notes already contain the exact intuition in a throwaway aside — g2_s2.html:336 'Sampling a person through a friendship link is sampling proportional to degree' (the friendship paradox). Connecting that aside to the Markov-chain theorem in G5 §3 would be a satisfying payoff across two notes.

One passing mention (g7_s3.html:903, 'multiplicative lognormal noise') with no PDF or moments. It slots naturally into the G3 §5 continuous zoo as a Y=e^X change-of-variables exercise, reinforcing G3 §4 machinery while explaining the multiplicative-noise remark G7 already makes.

Classic Stat 110 results with no 6.041 counterpart, but the notes already carry a full Beta definition box with the Beta function (g3_s3.html:461-462) and the Beta-Binomial conjugacy (g6_s3, g7_s5). enrichment.note: The notes use indicators heavily but only through linearity of expectation. The algebraic identities give inclusion-exclusion by indicators, which would pair well with the three-set inclusion-exclusion repair listed under partials — the two together make one coherent short addition to G1 §1 / G2 §5.

synthesis.coverage_summary:
189 merged items (~178 distinct after deduping cross-agent overlaps: Universality of the Uniform x2, uniform order statistics x2, graph random walk x2, reversibility x2, Jensen x2, binomial closure x2, chi-square x2, Gamma x2, and the MGF cluster counted across p2/p3/p8/p10).

By verdict: COVERED 128 (68%), PARTIAL 26 (14%), MISSING_OUT_OF_SYLLABUS 32 (17%), MISSING_IN_SYLLABUS 3 (1.6%).

The 32 out-of-syllabus items are dominated by three Stat 110 clusters: MGFs (9 items across the p3 section, the p8 example, and the p10 table column), order statistics (4), and Stat 110's extended named-distribution zoo plus its story-proof tooling (Negative Hypergeometric, capture-recapture, Beta-Gamma, MVN/bivariate-normal density, log-normal, indicator algebra, Simpson's paradox, the R command table, and Blitzstein's own resource links).

Which notes carry the load: G3 (continuous RVs, derived distributions, joint densities) is the workhorse — it alone answers most of cheatsheet p2, p3 col3, and p7; G5 fully covers the Markov-chain material on p4 col3, p5 and p8, at greater depth than the cheatsheet (mean recurrence via first-step analysis, the two failure modes of steady-state convergence); G4 covers all Poisson/Bernoulli-process and conditional-expectation material (p4) plus the discrete distribution families, again going further (splitting with the independence clause, competing exponentials with the winner's identity); G2 owns discrete RVs, indicators and the linearity examples on p7; G1 owns counting, conditioning and Bayes on p1; G6 owns LLN/CLT/Bayesian inference; G7 owns the classical-statistics material the cheatsheet only gestures at.

Three verdict conflicts were resolved by re-running greps against notes/src/fragments: (1) binomial closure — took MISSING over PARTIAL, confirmed no additivity statement exists; (2) chi-square — took the p7 agent's quoted evidence over the p6/p10 agents, since g7_s4.html:346-347 verifiably states both the n-squared-normals definition and E=n, Var=2n, so only placement is thin; (3) doubly stochastic and joint CDF — confirmed genuinely absent (zero grep hits), so both stand as real gaps.

items.topic: Common Mistake 6 — don't confuse a random variable with its distribution; PDF of X^2 needs a transformation, PDF of X+Y needs a convolution
items.detail: To get f_{X^2} use the transformation/CDF method, not (f_X)^2; to get f_{X+Y} compute f_{X+Y}(w)=\int f_X(x)f_Y(w-x)dx, not f_X+f_Y.
items.evidence: G3 §4 (derived distributions) and §5: grep -ri "convolution" hits 16 fragments including g3_s0..g3_s5. g3_s4.html:1150 states Exp(λ)+Exp(λ)=Erlang-2 with density λ^2 w e^{-λw} obtained by convolution; g3_s4.html:459 is Practice 4.8 ‘X standard normal, Y=X^2, find f_Y’ done by the CDF method; g7_s4.html:338 repeats the Z^2 transformation explicitly ('By the CDF method of …').

items.topic: Common Mistake 7 — E(g(X)) ≠ g(E(X)); use LOTUS
items.detail: E[g(X)] = Σ g(x)p_X(x) (or ∫ g(x)f_X(x)dx) — the expected value rule / LOTUS — and this generally differs from g(E[X]).
items.evidence: Course wording is 'expected value rule'; grep -ri "expected value rule|LOTUS" hits g2_s0, g2_s2, g2_s3, g2_s4, g3_s0, g3_s2, g4_s1, g4_s2. Worked contrast at g2_s2.html:125-126 (E[g(X)]=0.5208 vs g(E[X])=0.4 for g(x)=1/(x+1)), repeated continuously at g3_s3.html:639 (E[T]=4.620981 vs 200/E[V]=4.444444) and g5_s5.html:373 (E[24/W]=8.32 ≠ 24/E[W]=8, called 'the single most common lost-point on Quiz 2').

items.topic: Jensen's inequality (named in Mistake 7 as the explanation of the E(g(X)) vs g(E(X)) gap)
items.detail: For convex g, E[g(X)] ≥ g(E[X]); reversed for concave g.
items.evidence: Named five times but never stated as an inequality. g2_s2.html:126 explicitly defers it — 'a fact that gets a name (Jensen's inequality) later'; g3_s3.html:639 'the same Jensen gap'; g5_s5.html:373 'what Jensen and later the delta-method are about'; g5_s5.html:510 '1/w is convex (Jensen's inequality, and 8.317766>8)'; g7_s5.html:295 'not unbiased for σ, by Jensen's inequality (B&T §9.1)'. Grep for a formal statement ("convex" in g3_s3) found only an unrelated 'convex combination' at g3_s3.html:259. So the direction of the gap is always asserted per-example, never proved or stated in general.

items.evidence: Searched 'first ace', 'before the first Ace', 'negative hypergeometric', 'Negative Hypergeometric'. g1_s4.html:517 mentions aces only in a dealing/counting problem ('the first ace can go to any of the $4$ players'), and the many 'before the first' hits (g4_s3.html:786, g4_s4.html:418/429/438/973/994) are all Bernoulli/Poisson first-success problems, not this one. items.topic: Example: minimum and maximum of RVs - CDF of max of n i.i.d. Unif(0,1) is a^n
items.detail: $P(\max\le a)=\prod P(X_i\le a)$; $P(\min\ge a)=\prod P(X_i\ge a)$; for Unif(0,1), $F_{U_{(n)}}(a)=a^n$
items.evidence: Both directions are worked. g3_s1.html:554 'Practice: $F_M(m)=\mathbf{P}(X_1\le m)\mathbf{P}(X_2\le m)=(1-e^{-\lambda m})^2$ ... Differentiating with the chain rule, $f_M(m)=2(1-e^{-\lambda m})\lambda e^{-\lambda m}$' plus the tail-formula mean $3/(2\lambda)$. The uniform case verbatim: g7_s2.html:574-576 'Let $M=\max_i X_i$. For $0\le m\le\theta$, $F_M(m)=\mathbf{P}(X_1\le m,\dots,X_n\le m)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{P}(X_i\le m)=(m/\theta)^n$' (the MLE-for-$\theta$ example). Min-side via complement in the same sections.

items.topic: Example: pattern-matching with the e^x Taylor series - E(1/(X+1)) for X ~ Pois(lambda) via LOTUS

What is absent is the specific move of re-indexing an infinite LOTUS sum back into a recognisable $e^\lambda$ series; grep for 'pattern-match', 'Taylor series', '\\frac{1}{X+1}' turned up only unrelated Taylor expansions (g4_s3.html:127, g3_s5.html:366). Nice enrichment for series manipulation; not a 6.041 exam skill.

items.topic: Markov chain reversibility / detailed balance: s_i q_ij = s_j q_ji
items.detail: chain reversible w.r.t. $\vec s$ iff $s_iq_{ij}=s_jq_{ji}$ for all $i,j$
items.evidence: Detailed balance is present but only in the birth-death setting, and reversibility is never developed as a general property. g5_s5.html:230 'The cut (detailed balance) equation across the boundary between $i$ and $i+1$ is...' - this is the local-balance/cut argument used for queueing chains (g5_s3 Erlang-B, M/M/1). Reversibility itself appears once, in scare quotes and in passing: g5_s3.html:586 'chain that is "reversible"'. So a 6.041 learner gets the cut equations (which is what B&T Chapter 7 actually needs) but not the general reversibility criterion or the fact that it gives a shortcut to $\vec s$. B&T does not cover reversibility as such, so this is a soft gap.

items.topic: Markov chains (2): random walk on an undirected graph - stationary distribution proportional to degree
items.evidence: Searched 'random walk', 'degree', 'undirected', 'proportional to the degree'. items.topic: Universality of the Uniform (inverse-CDF transform)
items.evidence: grep 'universality of the uniform' -> 0 hits; grep 'inverse transform' -> 0 hits; grep 'inverse.{0,20}CDF' -> a single incidental hit in g4_s1. Not a B&T/6.041 topic (it belongs to simulation); worth adding only as optional enrichment alongside G3 §4 derived distributions.

items.topic: Normal distribution N(mu, sigma^2): standardization Z=(X-mu)/sigma ~ N(0,1), standard normal with CDF Phi, location-scale transformation closure
items.evidence: G3 §1 (normal pdf, standardization, Phi table) and G6 §2. grep 'standard normal' -> g3_s0/s1/s4 + g6_s1/s2/s4/s5 + all of g7; grep 'normal table' -> g3_s1, g3_s5, g6_s2, g7_s1/s2/s4; grep 'Phi(' -> 15 fragments. g3_s3 has 'linear function of a normal'. The cheatsheet's 'Location-Scale Transformation' is the course's aX+b closure of the normal family (aX+b: 14 hits in g3_s1).

items.topic: Normal is ubiquitous because of the CLT
items.evidence: G6 §2 is entirely the CLT: grep 'de Moivre' -> g6_s0/s2/s5 (de Moivre-Laplace), 'normal approximation' -> g6_s0/s1/s2 plus g7; g6_s2 also works the Poisson-versus-normal paradox from L20 slide 8. Far deeper than the cheatsheet's one sentence.

items.topic: Exponential distribution: story, rate parameter lambda, E[X]=1/lambda
items.evidence: G3 §1 (definition, pdf/CDF, mean/variance) and G4 §3-§4 (interarrival times of the Poisson process). grep 'exponential' hits 32 of 42 fragments; the rate-parameter reading ('1 per 1/4 hour on average') is the course's arrival-rate discussion in g4_s3.

items.topic: Memorylessness: P(X>s+t | X>s) = P(X>t); X-a | (X>a) ~ Expo(lambda); Exponential is the only continuous memoryless distribution
items.evidence: grep 'memoryless' -> 19 fragments, with 22 hits in g2_s3 (geometric memorylessness), 15 in g3_s1 (exponential memorylessness, the conditional-tail form), 16 in g4_s3, 9 in g4_s4. grep 'fresh-start' -> g2_s3, g4_s2 (14 hits), g4_s4 — the course's fresh-start property is exactly the cheatsheet's 'as good as new'.

items.topic: Expos as a rescaled Expo(1): Y~Expo(lambda) => lambda·Y ~ Expo(1)
items.evidence: The general machinery is covered — G3 §4 derived distributions handles Y=aX for continuous X (aX+b: 16 hits in g3_s4, 14 in g3_s1), and the exponential's scale-family behaviour is implicit throughout G4's rate arguments. But no fragment states the specific normalization 'lambda·X ~ Expo(1)' as a named, reusable fact.

items.topic: Min of Expos: min(X_1..X_k) ~ Expo(lambda_1+...+lambda_k)
items.evidence: grep 'minimum of.{0,20}exponential' -> g3_s1 (3 hits), g4_s4; grep 'competing exponential' -> g4_s4 (5 hits), g5_s5. g4_s4 states the full result including the winner's identity: 'min ~ Exp(sum_i lambda_i) and the winner is i with probability lambda_i/sum_j lambda_j, independently of the winning time' — strictly more than the cheatsheet.

items.topic: Max of Expos: max(X_1..X_k) ~ Y_1+...+Y_k with Y_j ~ Expo(j·lambda) independent
items.detail: the coupon-collector-style decomposition of the maximum into independent exponential stages
items.evidence: g3_s1 Example 1.7 (rec08 P3(d)) fully derives the CDF/pdf of Z=max{X_1,X_2,X_3} for iid Exp(lambda), including E[Z] via the tail formula. What is absent is the cheatsheet's *decomposition* identity max = sum of independent Expo(j·lambda) — a Stat 110 story-proof device rather than a 6.041 technique.

items.topic: Gamma(a, lambda) distribution: story as the total wait for the a-th arrival when interarrivals are Expo(lambda); the four PDF-shape figures
items.detail: Gamma(n,lambda) = sum of n iid Expo(lambda); general non-integer a requires the Gamma function
items.evidence: The integer case is covered exhaustively and by name: grep 'Erlang' -> g3_s4, g4_s0/s2/s3/s4/s5 (29 hits in g4_s4), g5_s3/s5, g6_s2, g7_s0/s1 — the k-th arrival time of a Poisson process, with pdf, mean k/lambda, variance k/lambda^2, and the bank-queue-style stories. What is thin: grep 'gamma distribution' -> 0 hits, grep 'Gamma function' -> 0 hits, so the general Gamma(a,lambda) with non-integer a is never named. This is a labelling gap, not a conceptual one, for 6.041.

items.topic: Beta(a,b) distribution and its PDF shapes
items.evidence: g3_s3 has a full 'Definition (beta distribution)' box: f(q)=q^{a-1}(1-q)^{b-1}/B(a,b) with the beta function B(a,b)=Gamma(a)Gamma(b)/Gamma(a+b)=(a-1)!(b-1)!/(a+b-1)! for integers, plus mean a/(a+b), mode (a-1)/(a+b-2) and variance. Arrived at from the recitation's coin-bias posterior.

items.topic: Conjugate prior of the Binomial: X|p ~ Bin(n,p), p ~ Beta(a,b) => p|(X=x) ~ Beta(a+x, b+n-x)
items.evidence: g3_s3 derives the Beta posterior from a Beta prior under Bernoulli/binomial observation (the recitation coin-bias example, then the general Beta definition box). g6_s3 discusses conjugacy explicitly (5 hits), including a Gotcha: 'Two of our three canonical calculations were conjugate — beta prior stays beta under binomial data, normal prior stays normal under normal noise', plus a counterexample warning that conjugacy is the exception. The updating rule a->a+x, b->b+n-x is present in the worked posterior ('8/12 instead of 7/10' pseudo-count reading).

items.topic: Order statistics of the Uniform
items.evidence: grep 'order statistic' -> 0 hits in all 42 fragments. Not in B&T/6.041 (only min and max appear, in G3 §4 derived distributions). Optional enrichment.

items.topic: Beta-Gamma relationship / bank-post office result: X~Gamma(a,l), Y~Gamma(b,l) independent => X/(X+Y) ~ Beta(a,b) and X+Y independent of X/(X+Y)
items.detail: X/(X+Y) ~ Beta(a,b),  X+Y  independent of  X/(X+Y)
items.evidence: grep 'bank' / 'post office' / 'X/(X+Y)' -> no relevant hits; grep 'beta distribution' -> g3_s3 only (definition, no Gamma link). A classic Stat 110 result with no 6.041 counterpart.

items.topic: Chi-Square distribution: chi^2_n = Z_1^2+...+Z_n^2 for iid standard normals; chi^2_n = Gamma(n/2, 1/2)
items.detail: X ~ chi^2_n  <=>  X = sum_{i=1}^n Z_i^2,  Z_i iid N(0,1);  equivalently Gamma(n/2, 1/2)
items.evidence: g3_s4 Practice 4.8 derives the chi-square density with ONE degree of freedom from Y=X^2, X standard normal: f_Y(y)=(1/sqrt(2 pi y))e^{-y/2}, and names it. g7_s4 uses chi^2_r heavily (16 'chi-square' hits) for the generalized-likelihood-ratio / goodness-of-fit test, including the correct rank-(m-1) projection argument and 'The squared norm of a mean-zero Gaussian with a rank-r projection covariance is exactly chi^2_r'. What is missing is the plain definition 'chi^2_n = sum of n squared standard normals' stated up front, and the Gamma(n/2,1/2) identification.

items.topic: Table: distributions for four sampling schemes (Binomial / HGeom / NBin / NHGeom by replace vs no-replace x fixed-n vs draw-until-r)
items.detail: 2x2 table: Replace+fixed n = Binomial (Bern if n=1); No-replace+fixed n = HGeom; Replace+until r successes = NBin (Geom if r=1); No-replace+until r = NHGeom
items.evidence: Three of the four cells are covered individually and well — Binomial/Bernoulli in g2_s1, Hypergeometric in g1_s4 Example 4.14 (full urn derivation) and g2_s1 (explicitly contrasted with the binomial: 'the draws are not independent... It is the hypergeometric PMF'), NBin/Pascal in g4_s2. But grep 'sampling scheme' -> only two incidental hits (g2_s2, g5_s5) and there is no unifying 2x2 organizing table. NHGeom is out of 6.041 scope. The gap is the *organizing device*, not the content.

items.topic: Bernoulli distribution: story, indicator of success, 1-X ~ Bern(1-p)
items.evidence: g2_s1 has an explicit 'Definition (Bernoulli; B&T §2.2 p. 75)' box. Indicator random variables are a major theme: grep 'indicator' -> 30 hits in g2_s4, 24 in g2_s5, plus g2_s1, g6_s1, g7_s2 (indicator decomposition for expectations).

items.topic: Binomial distribution: story, X = X_1+...+X_n as a sum of iid Bernoullis, PMF figure
items.evidence: g2_s1 derives the binomial PMF with the counting/independence argument and includes the B&T Figure 2.3 shape discussion (Fig. 1.2 panel (c), n=10 at p=0.2/0.5/0.8, symmetry, peak near np). g2_s1 also has 'binomial ... sum of' (the Bernoulli-sum representation). 'binomial' hits 29 of 42 fragments.

items.topic: Binomial property — Redefine success: n - X ~ Bin(n, 1-p)
items.evidence: g2_s1's shape discussion works exactly this symmetry: 'swapping the roles of H and T maps k -> n-k and leaves the formula unchanged. ... The p=0.2 and p=0.8 curves are exact mirror images'. Stated as a symmetry rather than as a labelled property, but the content is there.

items.topic: Binomial property — Sum: X~Bin(n,p), Y~Bin(m,p) independent => X+Y ~ Bin(n+m, p)
items.evidence: grep 'sum of two independent binomial' -> 0 hits; 'binomial.{0,80}binomial.{0,40}sum' -> 0 hits; 'Bin.n[+]m' -> 0 hits. The general tool (discrete convolution) is thoroughly covered in G3 §4 (25 'convolution' hits in g3_s4), and the Poisson analogue IS stated via merging in G4 §4, so the binomial closure fact is a small, in-scope omission — a natural worked convolution example that would also reinforce the Bernoulli-sum picture.

items.topic: Binomial conditional: X | (X+Y=r) ~ HGeom(n, m, r)
items.detail: conditioning two independent binomials on their total gives a hypergeometric
items.evidence: grep 'conditional.{0,60}hypergeom' and 'hypergeom.{0,80}conditional' -> 0 hits; g2_s4's 'conditional ... binomial' hits are about conditional PMFs generally, not this identity. A Stat 110 story-proof result; B&T never states it.

items.topic: Binomial-Poisson relationship: Bin(n,p) ~= Pois(lambda) when p is small
items.evidence: grep 'Poisson approximation' -> g4_s3 (3 hits), g6_s2. G4 §3 builds the whole Bernoulli->Poisson limit as the course's central construction, with the Fig. 3.5 Bernoulli/Poisson dictionary ('the third row (binomial -> Poisson: counts)') and the p = lambda·delta -> 0 scaling made explicit.

items.topic: Binomial-Normal relationship: Bin(n,p) ~= N(np, np(1-p)) for large n, p not near 0 or 1
items.evidence: G6 §2. grep 'de Moivre' -> g6_s0, g6_s2 (7 hits), g6_s5; grep 'continuity correction' -> g6_s0, g7_s4, and g6_s2 works the correction numerically (z=200.5 cut, comparing corrected 0.063259 vs exact 0.065206 vs uncorrected 0.068019). Deeper than the cheatsheet.

items.topic: Geometric distribution (cheatsheet convention: number of FAILURES before the first success)
items.evidence: G2 §1/§3. grep 'geometric.{0,30}number of (trials|failures)' -> g2_s1 (2), g2_s3. Note the convention shift: B&T/6.041 defines the geometric as the number of trials up to AND INCLUDING the first success (mean 1/p), the cheatsheet as failures before it (mean (1-p)/p). Both parameterizations and the shift-by-one relation are handled in g2_s1/g2_s3 and reused in G4 §2 (9 'first success' hits in g4_s2).

items.topic: First Success distribution: FS(p) = Geom(p)+1, E[X]=1/p
items.evidence: This IS the course's geometric distribution. grep 'first success' -> g2_s1 (8), g2_s3 (4), g2_s5, g4_s2 (9), g4_s3, g4_s5, g5_s5, g7_s2; E[X]=1/p is derived in G2 §3 and reused as the interarrival mean throughout G4 §2 and in g5_s4 ('the wait is geometric with parameter 0.6 and mean 1/0.6').

items.topic: Negative Binomial NBin(r,p): number of failures before the r-th success
items.evidence: g4_s2 states the Pascal PMF of order k as a theorem box: p_{Y_k}(t)=C(t-1,k-1)p^k(1-p)^{t-k}, with E[Y_k]=k/p and var=k(1-p)/p^2, derived as a sum of k iid geometrics, and explicitly notes 'also called the negative binomial'. grep 'Pascal' -> g1_s4, g4_s0 (5), g4_s2 (18), g4_s3 (4), g4_s5 (5). Again the trials-vs-failures convention differs by k.

items.topic: Hypergeometric HGeom(w,b,n): story (sampling without replacement), PMF, the standard examples
items.evidence: g1_s4 Example 4.14 (rec04 P3, B&T Problem 1.61) derives the general urn answer for i red out of k drawn from n balls with m red, flagged as a solution-gap the notes fill in. g2_s1 works a small numeric case and uses it as 'the standing counterexample when §1.4 tempts you to call every count binomial'. grep 'without replacement' -> g1_s2, g1_s4 (7), g1_s5 (3), g2_s1 (4), g2_s5.

items.topic: Capture-recapture (HGeom(n, N-n, m) tagged-elk example)
items.detail: tag n of N elk, recapture m; number tagged ~ HGeom(n, N-n, m)
items.evidence: grep 'capture.recapture' -> 0 hits (the 'capture' hits in g4_s4/g6 are the ordinary English verb). Purely an application flavour of the hypergeometric already covered; Stat 110 staple, not a 6.041 one.

items.topic: Poisson distribution Pois(lambda): rare-events story, accidents-per-month example
items.evidence: g2_s4 introduces the Poisson PMF/mean/variance; G4 §3-§4 is an entire treatment of the Poisson process with the rare-events limit story spelled out. grep 'poisson' -> 21 fragments.

items.topic: Poisson property — Sum: X~Pois(l1), Y~Pois(l2) independent => X+Y ~ Pois(l1+l2)
items.evidence: This is the course's MERGING of Poisson processes. grep 'merging' -> g2_s0, g2_s3, g3_s4, g4_s0, g4_s2, g4_s3, g4_s4, g4_s5, g5_s1, g5_s5; g4_s3 Fig. 3.5 lists merging as a dictionary row 'previewed here and proved in §4'. lambda_1 + lambda_2 arithmetic appears 32x in g4_s4.

items.topic: Poisson property — Conditional: X | (X+Y=n) ~ Bin(n, l1/(l1+l2))
items.evidence: g4_s4's decision list states it directly: 'Given a count, how are arrivals distributed among types? Binomial (two types) or multinomial'. g4_s3 has 'conditioned on the total'. The same fragment gives the companion competing-exponential result lambda_i/sum_j lambda_j.

items.topic: Poisson property — Chicken-egg / thinning: accept each of Z~Pois(l) items w.p. p => accepted ~ Pois(lp), rejected ~ Pois(l(1-p)), and the two are INDEPENDENT
items.evidence: This is the course's SPLITTING of a Poisson process. grep 'splitting.{0,40}Poisson' -> g4_s4 (5 hits), g4_s5, g5_s5; grep 'thinning' -> g4_s2, g4_s3, g5_s5. g4_s4 states the full result including the independence clause: 'the label-i stream is Poisson at rate p_i·lambda, and the label streams are mutually independent' — the independence is the surprising part and the notes have it.

items.topic: Multinomial distribution Mult_k(n, p): story and joint PMF n!/(n_1!...n_k!) p_1^{n_1}...p_k^{n_k}
items.evidence: g1_s4 §4.6 derives the multinomial coefficient by the slot argument (rec04 P4) and computes multinomial probabilities (rec04 P5) — 18 'multinomial' hits. g7_s4 restates the joint PMF as p_X(x;theta)=c·theta_1^{n_1}...theta_m^{n_m} with c=n!/(n_1!...n_m!) for the goodness-of-fit derivation.

items.topic: Multinomial marginals, lumping, and conditionals: X_i ~ Bin(n,p_i); X_i+X_j ~ Bin(n, p_i+p_j); lumped categories stay Multinomial; X_1..X_{k-1} | X_k=n_k ~ Mult_{k-1}(n-n_k, p/(1-p_k))
items.detail: marginal Bin(n,p_i); lumping closure; conditional renormalized Multinomial
items.evidence: g7_s4 states the marginal fact ('Marginally N_k ~ Bin(n, theta_k^*)') and uses it, so the marginal half is present. But grep found no statement of the lumping-closure property or the conditional-Multinomial property anywhere in g1_s4/g1_s5/g4_s4/g7_s4. Lumping in particular is a genuinely useful counting move that fits G1 §4 and G2's joint-PMF marginalization.

items.topic: Multinomial variances and covariances: Var(X_i)=n p_i(1-p_i), Cov(X_i,X_j) = -n p_i p_j
items.detail: Cov(X_i, X_j) = -n p_i p_j  for i != j
items.evidence: g7_s4 gives var(N_k;H_0)=n·theta_k^*(1-theta_k^*) and, in the chi-square limit argument, the asymptotic covariance matrix Sigma = I - sqrt(theta)sqrt(theta)^T with 'off-diagonal entries -sqrt(theta_j theta_k)'. So the *negative* covariance structure is present in asymptotic (normalized) form, but the plain exact identity Cov(X_i,X_j) = -n p_i p_j is never stated. It is squarely in scope — G3 §5 covers covariance and G2 §5 covers indicator decompositions, which is exactly how you prove it.

items.topic: Multivariate Uniform: on a 2D region probability is proportional to area, density = 1/(area of region); 3D analogue by volume
items.evidence: G3 §2 is built on this: grep 'uniform on.{0,30}(region|square|triangle|disk|circle)' -> g1_s1, g3_s2 (18 hits), g3_s4; 'Unif' appears 81x in g3_s2. Joint uniform densities over regions, with marginals and conditionals obtained by area ratios, are the section's running examples.

items.topic: Multivariate Normal: definition via 'every linear combination is Normal', mean vector and covariance matrix; any subvector is MVN
items.detail: t_1X_1+...+t_kX_k Normal for all t  <=>  X is MVN
items.evidence: grep 'multivariate normal' -> g6_s3 (a posterior recognized as N(mu,Sigma) after completing the square in the linear-Gaussian model) and g7_s4 (the multivariate CLT limit in the goodness-of-fit derivation). Both USE an MVN, neither DEFINES the family or states the subvector/linear-combination characterization. B&T 6.041 does not develop MVN theory; the linear-Gaussian cases the course needs are already handled. Enrichment only.

items.topic: MVN property: within an MVN, uncorrelated => independent
items.evidence: The converse warning is emphatic — g3_s4 Gotcha: '"Zero covariance" and "uncorrelated" mean the same thing, and neither means independent', with Example 4.9 as the counterexample. But the jointly-normal EXCEPTION is never stated. The closest is g6_s4's theorem 'If Theta and X are jointly normal, then E[Theta|X] is an affine function of X ... var(Theta|X=x)=(1-rho^2)sigma_Theta^2 for every x' — which implies the rho=0 case but does not say it. Given how strongly the notes warn that uncorrelated != independent, one sentence naming the normal exception is a real (if small) in-scope repair.

items.topic: Bivariate Normal joint PDF for N(0,1) marginals with correlation rho
items.evidence: grep 'bivariate normal' -> a single hit in g6_s4, and only as the caption of a scatter figure ('Scatter of 4000 samples from a bivariate normal with correlation 0.8') illustrating linear LMS — the density formula never appears. B&T 6.041 does not require the bivariate normal density; the course gets what it needs from the jointly-normal LLMS theorem in g6_s4. Optional enrichment for G3 §5 / G6 §4.

items.evidence: No 'MGF' hits. 6.041 proves distributional identities (e.g. sum of normals, sum of Poissons) by convolution instead — see g3_s4 §4.7 'The sum of two independent normals is normal'.

items.evidence: No 'MGF' hits. The same job is done in our notes by convolution: g3_s4 §4.5 'Discrete convolution', §4.6 'Continuous convolution and the sum of two uniforms', §4.7 sum of two independent normals (25 'convolution' hits in g3_s4).

items.topic: Joint CDF of two RVs: F(x,y) = P(X ≤ x, Y ≤ y)
items.evidence: Grep 'F_\{X,Y\}|joint CDF|joint cumulative|bivariate CDF' over all fragments → No matches. Grep of the 6 'CDF' occurrences in g3_s2.html (the joint-PDF section) shows all are one-variable CDFs (exponential CDF, P(Z≤z)=z²). The only 2-D CDF symbol in the whole corpus is an incidental $F_{R,\Theta}$ in g4_s1.html:518 inside a polar-coordinates example, never defined. B&T §3.4 does state the joint CDF, so this is in scope.

items.evidence: The identity appears exactly once, un-flagged, mid-derivation in g4_s1.html:518 ($f_{R,\Theta}=\partial^2 F_{R,\Theta}/\partial r\partial\theta$). g3_s2 §2.1 'The joint PDF, and probability as volume' defines the joint PDF directly as a density integrated over regions and never states the CDF↔PDF differentiation link in 2-D. Thin: a learner has the 1-D $f=F'$ (g3_s1) but no stated 2-D analogue.
